references.text: Isaiah describes the fire that is not quenched: 'their fire shall not be quenched' ([ref:Jes 66:24|Isaiah 66:24]). The rich man's torment in the flames reflects this eschatological judgment.
The previous verse ([ref:Luk 16:23|Luke 16:23]) sets the scene: the rich man is in Hades and sees Abraham far away with Lazarus at his side, which motivates his cry in verse 24.
Abraham's answer in [ref:Luk 16:25-26|Luke 16:25–26] rejects the rich man's plea by pointing to the great chasm and noting that he received his good things during his life.
Jesus warns about Gehenna where 'the fire is not quenched' ([ref:Mark 9:43-48|Mark 9:43–48]). The rich man's suffering in the flames illustrates this same reality.
The lake of fire in [ref:Åp 20:15|Revelation 20:15] is the final judgment for those not written in the book of life, which corresponds with the rich man's torment in the flames.
Abraham is called 'father' by the rich man, just as Abraham is the patriarch of Israel ([ref:1 Mos 18:27|Genesis 18:27]). The address 'Father Abraham' points to this Jewish claim of heritage.
John the Baptist warns against relying on Abraham being a father: 'We have Abraham as our father' ([ref:Luk 3:8|Luke 3:8]). The rich man's appeal to Abraham as his father does not help him.
The wretched and poor seek water but find none ([ref:Jes 41:17|Isaiah 41:17]). The rich man desperately begs for a drop of water—an ironic reversal where the rich one is now the needy one.

Zechariah describes a plague where flesh rots while people stand—God's judgment on enemies ([ref:Sak 14:12|Zechariah 14:12]). The motif of physical torment in God's judgment corresponds with the rich man's suffering.

Those who worship the beast 'will be tormented with fire and sulfur … the smoke of their torment rises forever' ([ref:Åp 14:10-11|Revelation 14:10–11]). The motif of eternal torment in fire parallels the rich man's suffering in the flames.

Jesus says to those on his left: 'Depart from me, you cursed, into the eternal fire' ([ref:Matt 25:41|Matthew 25:41]). The rich man, who ignored Lazarus in need, represents exactly those who showed no mercy.
